title: Australian Tattoo Artists Condemn Bali General Anesthetic Body Art Trend
text: Australian Tattoo Artists Condemn Bali General Anesthetic Body Art Trend Experts warn against Bali's controversial trend of full-body tattoos under general anaesthetic, citing high costs, severe medical risks, and the loss of the art form's transformative value. A prominent Sydney tattoo master has issued a scathing critique of the growing trend among Australian tourists visiting Bali to undergo full-body tattooing procedures under general anaesthetic. Kian Forreal, the owner and master artist at Authentink Studio located in Surry Hills, described the practice as fundamentally flawed and dangerous. He compared the experience to taking a helicopter to the summit of Mount Everest and claiming to have climbed it, arguing that it strips the art form of its essential transformative nature. High Costs And Hospital Settings For Body ArtTourists are currently paying between $9,000 and $16,000 for these extensive sessions, a price that covers hospital fees and medical procedures. These operations take place in licensed hospital operating rooms in Bali, where up to nine different artists work on a single client simultaneously. The intense sessions last between 10 and 20 hours, condensing work that would typically require months or years of traditional appointments into one or two visits.Thousands of travelers have flocked to the Indonesian island this year specifically for large or full-body tattoos. Social media posts showcasing the procedure have gone viral, fueling interest in what seems like a convenient alternative. Bali is already a major destination for affordable ink, with foreigners accounting for at least 80 percent of tattoo shop clients on the island.Artists Critique Quality And Transformative ValueForreal, who has 33 years of experience specializing in traditional Japanese Irezumi and large-scale bodysuits, questioned the artistic quality of these rapid procedures. He stated that clients usually receive what he described as AI or Pinterest slop mashed together, rather than a cohesive piece of art. He emphasized that properly executed tattoos are something earned through endurance, contrasting sharply with the anesthesia-assisted approach.He noted that during the 100 hours he typically spends with clients in four- to six-hour chunks, they undergo a personal transformation. Forreal explained that clients cannot call in sick because they squirm, sweat, and bleed, but they push through it. This struggle is integral to the experience, creating a sense of earned placement within the tattoo community. He argued that getting a giant dragon tattoo to appear tough is meaningless if the person cannot sit through the process.Other Sydney-based professionals share these concerns. Ray Vom, who runs Markd Tattoo Studio in Redfern, condemned the trend as a massive risk that is not sufficiently stressed to the public. He warned that some people do not wake up from the anaesthetic. Kristen Sorrenson from Nine Muses on the Gold Coast also stated she would not take those odds to get a tattoo, prioritizing her safety over the aesthetic outcome.Medical Professionals Warn Of Severe Health RisksMedical experts have joined artists in condemning the practice, labeling it dangerous, unnecessary, and unsafe. Kyle Hoath, president of the Australian Medical Association WA, explained that general anaesthetic requires a trained medical professional to keep a patient breathing and alive while unconscious. He highlighted that the procedure carries significant risks, including the potential for death.Doctors generally avoid using general anaesthetic for procedures that can be performed safely without it. Hoath stated that while tattooing can be done in safe sterile environments, adding general anaesthetic introduces considerable risk for mere convenience. He described the practice as an unnecessary complication that should be avoided, noting that such procedures are not seen in Australia and likely never will be accepted there.Despite these strong warnings from both the artistic and medical communities, tourists predominantly from Australia continue to travel to Bali seeking faster, cheaper, and pain-free full-body tattoos. Brisbane man Anthony Waud visited the island in September and spent nine hours under general anaesthetic to have his front and back tattooed.Waud reported that he paid $9,000 for the entire process and experienced no problems with his recovery. However, his experience represents just one side of a controversial phenomenon that experts argue compromises both artistic integrity and personal safety. The trend highlights a growing disconnect between consumer desire for immediate, pain-free results and the established standards of the tattoo industry and medical ethics.
